word:greek-nt:G0135.explanation: This word describes an “obscure thing” or a “poor reflection”—something that does not give a clear, complete view. Its central idea is limited or imperfect perception: what is seen is real enough to resemble the truth, yet not fully clear. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 13:12. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its meaning points to obscurity or an incomplete reflection.

word:greek-nt:G0179.explanation: This word means “indestructible”: it describes something that cannot be destroyed or brought to an end. It points to lasting permanence rather than something temporary, fragile, or subject to decay. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 7:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the quality of being incapable of destruction or ending.

word:greek-nt:G0207.explanation: Akylas is a male personal name.

word:greek-nt:G0333.explanation: This word means to contemplate something closely—to look carefully at it rather than give it only a passing glance. It describes attentive consideration or examination, whether directed toward something seen or toward its significance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts and Hebrews. Its basic idea is deliberate, focused attention: observing carefully and reflecting on what is being considered. The surrounding verse determines what is being examined and what response that careful attention calls for.

word:greek-nt:G0386.explanation: Anastasis means rising again or resurrection.

word:greek-nt:G0416.explanation: This word describes something being blown or moved by the wind. It presents wind as the force carrying or shifting an object, rather than describing the object’s own deliberate movement. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in James 1:6, and its ordinary meaning is “be wind-blown” or “to be moved by the wind.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central picture is something unstable because the wind drives it.

word:greek-nt:G0508.explanation: This word means “an upper room,” referring to a room located above the main level of a building. It is a straightforward place-word rather than a description of an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Mark 14:15 and once in Luke 22:12. The surrounding passage determines what happens in that room, but the word itself identifies its elevated location.

word:greek-nt:G0531.explanation: The word means “permanent”: lasting, enduring, and not temporary. It describes something that continues rather than passing away or changing quickly. This Greek New Testament word appears once, in Hebrews 7:24. Its basic sense is clear, but the exact way it applies in that verse must be understood from the surrounding sentence and passage. It expresses lasting continuance, not a brief or momentary condition.

word:greek-nt:G0544.explanation: Apeitheō means to disobey. It can also describe refusing conformity, as when people do not obey the Son or the truth.

word:greek-nt:G0629.explanation: Apolytrosis means release secured by a ransom payment: redemption or deliverance.

word:greek-nt:G0665.explanation: Apotrepo means to turn away from or shun.

word:greek-nt:G0760.explanation: This Greek New Testament word is a personal name, referring to “Asa” or “Asaph.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs two times in the Greek New Testament, both in Matthew 1:7–8. Since it is a name, its basic meaning is the person identified by that name; the surrounding verse supplies any further significance. “Asa” and “Asaph” are the two approved renderings associated with this name.

word:greek-nt:G0782.explanation: Aspazomai means to greet or salute someone.

word:greek-nt:G0827.explanation: Auge means brightness, daylight, or dawn, as in the break of day.

word:greek-nt:G0885.explanation: Akim is a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it identifies a person named in Matthew’s genealogy. The name appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both occurrences being in Matthew 1:14, though the passage text is not provided here. As a name, Akim does not itself describe a virtue, action, or teaching; its meaning in a particular verse comes from the person and surrounding genealogy in which it appears.

word:greek-nt:G0922.explanation: Baros means a weight or burden.

word:greek-nt:G1024.explanation: Brachus means little or few. It can also describe a short span of time.

word:greek-nt:G1051.explanation: Gala means milk. It can refer to milk from a flock.

word:greek-nt:G1068.explanation: Gethsemane is the name of a place.

word:greek-nt:G1136.explanation: Gog is a name associated with Magog. Here, Gog and Magog are named among the nations gathered for war.

word:greek-nt:G1183.explanation: Dekatoō means to tithe, or to collect a tenth.

word:greek-nt:G1213.explanation: Dēloō means to make something clear or reveal it.

word:greek-nt:G1330.explanation: Dierchomai means to pass through or go through. It describes moving through a place, such as passing through Samaria and Galilee.

word:greek-nt:G1477.explanation: This word means “foundation”: something that provides a firm basis or support. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Timothy 3:15. Its central idea is a stable base on which something rests or is established. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be explained beyond this basic meaning. Its lexical meaning is nevertheless clear: it points to a foundation or firm supporting basis.

word:greek-nt:G1594.explanation: Eknēphō means to wake up—to come to one's senses.

word:greek-nt:G1666.explanation: Elisha is the personal name represented by this Greek New Testament word. It identifies Elisha rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 4:27, and its English rendering is “Elisha.” As a proper name, it functions chiefly to identify the person named, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular context.

word:greek-nt:G1712.explanation: This word refers to a market or marketplace—a public place connected with buying, selling, and trade. Its meaning can include the commercial activity associated with such a place, not merely the physical location. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 2:16, and is rendered “marketplace.” The word therefore identifies a setting where commerce takes place. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a marketplace or place of trade.

word:greek-nt:G1873.explanation: Epakouo means to hear or listen to.

word:greek-nt:G1910.explanation: Epibainō means to set foot on or step onto something. It can also mean to mount an animal or board a ship.

word:greek-nt:G2025.explanation: Epichriō means to spread on or anoint.

word:greek-nt:G2069.explanation: Esli is a personal name preserved as “Esli” in English. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 3:25. The word identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. Its significance in that verse is best understood from the surrounding passage and the person being named, rather than by assigning it an additional meaning not given here.

word:greek-nt:G2087.explanation: Heteros means another or other. It marks a second person or thing in relation to one already mentioned.

word:greek-nt:G2142.explanation: Euporia means wealth, gain, or plenty.

word:greek-nt:G2256.explanation: This word means “half an hour,” referring to a period of thirty minutes. It expresses a measured span of time rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 8:1. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while its specific significance in that passage belongs to the wider context. Its single occurrence makes it a precise time expression rather than a broadly recurring biblical term.

word:greek-nt:G2304.explanation: This word means “divine,” describing what belongs to, comes from, or is associated with God. It functions as a describing word, marking something as having a God-related character rather than an ordinary human one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Acts and twice in 2 Peter. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a direct reference to what is divine.

word:greek-nt:G2348.explanation: Thnēskō means to die or to be dead.

word:greek-nt:G2371.explanation: Thumomacheō means to be furiously angry with someone, as Herod was with the people of Tyre and Sidon.

word:greek-nt:G2418.explanation: This word describes carrying out sacred service, especially the work of serving in a priestly capacity. Its central meaning is “to minister” or “to perform priestly duty,” presenting the action as an active service rather than merely a title or role. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 15:16. The surrounding verse provides the context for how this sacred service is being described, but the word itself focuses on performing ministry or priestly work.

word:greek-nt:G2421.explanation: Iessai means Jesse. Jesse was Obed’s son and David’s father.

word:greek-nt:G2454.explanation: This word means “Judaism,” referring to the Jewish religious identity and way of life. It names the religious system or commitment associated with being Jewish, rather than describing a single action or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, and both occurrences are in Galatians 1:13–14. Its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding verse context, but its central sense remains Judaism.

word:greek-nt:G2537.explanation: Kainos means fresh or new. It describes new wine and a new covenant.

word:greek-nt:G2595.explanation: Karphos means a small piece, such as a speck in the eye.

word:greek-nt:G2623.explanation: Katakleio means to shut up or confine.

word:greek-nt:G2696.explanation: This word means “to be sealed up” or “to seal.” It describes something closed or secured with a seal, indicating that access or opening has been restricted. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 5:1. The word itself expresses the act or condition of sealing, while the surrounding verse determines what has been sealed and why that matters. Its basic idea is firm closure or secure restriction, rather than merely covering or shutting something casually.

word:greek-nt:G2788.explanation: Kithara means a harp or lyre, a musical instrument played to produce sound.

word:greek-nt:G2919.explanation: Krino means to judge. It can also mean to decide what is right or to be judged in a legal matter.

word:greek-nt:G2955.explanation: Kyptō means to bend or stoop down.

word:greek-nt:G3134.explanation: This form means “our lord has come,” “our lord comes,” or “our lord is at hand.”

word:greek-nt:G3178.explanation: Methe means deep drinking or drunkenness.

word:greek-nt:G3439.explanation: Monogenēs means only, only-begotten, or unique. It can describe an only child, such as a mother’s only son or a father’s only daughter.

word:greek-nt:G3581.explanation: Xenos means a stranger or foreigner. It can also describe something strange.

word:greek-nt:G3747.explanation: Osteon means a bone or bones.

word:greek-nt:G3884.explanation: Paralogizomai means to deceive or mislead. It can describe beguiling someone with persuasive words. It can also describe deceiving oneself.

word:greek-nt:G3963.explanation: Patmos is a place name, referring to a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Revelation 1:9, and the English rendering is “Patmos.” Because the available wording identifies the place but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the wider context.

word:greek-nt:G4081.explanation: This word means “clay,” “mud,” or “of clay.” It refers to soft, earthy material that can be handled or formed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times: five occurrences are in John and one is in Romans. Its central meaning remains the same in each occurrence—a substance made from earth, whether described as clay or mud in English translations.

word:greek-nt:G4139.explanation: Plesion means a neighbor—someone near or nearby.

word:greek-nt:G4175.explanation: This word means “citizenship,” referring to a person’s civic belonging or status as a citizen. It names the community or realm to which someone belongs, rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Philippians 3:20. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to citizenship and the belonging that citizenship expresses.

word:greek-nt:G4247.explanation: This word refers to an older woman or old woman. It is a specific description of a female person who is advanced in age, rather than a general word for any woman. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 2:3. Its exact role in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but the word itself identifies the person as an older woman. The central meaning remains straightforward: a woman who is older in years.

word:greek-nt:G4302.explanation: Prolegō means to tell beforehand or forewarn.

word:greek-nt:G4434.explanation: Ptochos means poor or destitute. It can also describe those who are poor in spirit.

word:greek-nt:G4441.explanation: Pynthanomai means to ask or inquire to obtain information or understanding. It can describe asking what something means or inquiring about when an event occurred.

word:greek-nt:G4517.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “farewell” and “to be strong.” It is a parting expression that can convey the wish that someone remain well, steady, or strong as they go. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 15:29. Its basic sense is therefore a closing greeting or farewell rather than a description of an object, person, or action repeated throughout the New Testament.

word:greek-nt:G4650.explanation: This form means to scatter or disperse.

word:greek-nt:G4852.explanation: Symphēmi means to consent or agree, as in agreeing that the law is good.

word:greek-nt:G4926.explanation: This word means “to converse” or “to talk with,” describing direct spoken interaction between people. It functions as a verb, pointing to the act of speaking with someone rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 10:27. Its basic sense is simply conversation or personal communication; the surrounding verse determines the particular subject and tone of that conversation.

word:greek-nt:G4993.explanation: Sōphroneō means to be of sound mind or sober-minded. It describes thinking in a right and measured way rather than thinking more highly of oneself than one should.

word:greek-nt:G5011.explanation: Tapeinos means humble or lowly in spirit. It can also describe a person in humble or lowly circumstances.

word:greek-nt:G5028.explanation: Taphos means a tomb or grave.

word:greek-nt:G5184«G5183.explanation: Τυρίοις means Tyrian, referring to people of Tyre.

word:greek-nt:G5222.explanation: Hypantēsis means a meeting. It describes people going out to meet someone.

word:greek-nt:G5385.explanation: Philosophia means philosophy, or love of wisdom.

word:greek-nt:G5446.explanation: This word means “natural,” describing what belongs to nature, follows natural origin, or has the character of what is natural. It functions as an adjective, so it identifies a person, thing, or action in relation to nature rather than presenting a separate action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Romans and 2 Peter. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

word:greek-nt:G5572.explanation: This word refers to a false teacher—someone presented as a teacher whose teaching is false. It is a plural noun, so it can describe more than one such teacher. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Peter 2:1. The basic meaning identifies the person by the character of the teaching: these are teachers associated with falsehood rather than truth. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what those teachers did in that verse.

word:greek-nt:G5590.explanation: Psychē means life, and it can also mean soul.

word:greek-nt:G6003.explanation: This word means “to assemble” or “to assemble together”—to bring people into one gathered group. It emphasizes coming together rather than remaining separated. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Luke 24:33. The word’s basic sense is straightforward: people are gathered together in one place or community. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a collective assembling.
